# Helping Your Midwife Find You

### A little guide from the Riverside Community Midwives

Hello! If you are reading this, you are planning to have your baby at home. That's lovely, and we are very happy to be part of it.

In the Philippines we say the midwife is like family, and that is how we want you to think of us. When you ring, we are not strangers coming to your house. We are coming as a friend. But even friends get lost sometimes, especially at 3 o'clock in the morning, in the rain, on a street where every house looks the same.

So this page is about one simple thing: **helping us get to you, and get inside, as fast as possible.** Some of it is common sense and some of it we learned the hard way. Please read it, show it to your partner or birth partner, and stick the checklist on the fridge.

---

## First, the important bit: 37 weeks

**Home birth cover starts from 37 weeks.**

Before 37 weeks, your baby is not ready to be born at home. If labour starts before then, you need to go to the **hospital**, not wait for us at home. Please use the hospital number in your notes.

We tell everyone this at the booking visit, but it's a long time from booking to birth and lots of people forget. So we're telling you again. And again. Write it on the calendar!

---

## When labour starts: how to call us

**Ring the Riverside Birth Line:** [BIRTH LINE NUMBER]

Please ring the **birth line**, not your midwife's own mobile.

We know it's tempting. You have got to know your midwife, you have her number, she's lovely. But she might be asleep, on holiday, or at another birth on the other side of Liverpool. The birth line always goes to **whoever is on call**, so someone will always answer and someone will always come.

When you ring, have these ready:

- Your name and date of birth
- How many weeks pregnant you are
- Your **full address**, including flat number, block name and postcode
- Anything we need to know to find you (see below!)

**In an emergency, ring 999.** Don't wait for us.

---

## Two midwives, two cars

For the birth, **two midwives** will come to you. Usually we come in **separate cars**, at different times.

So if you can, please keep **two parking spaces** free near your door. Ask a neighbour to move their car, put your own car round the corner, or just keep the drive clear.

Why does it matter? Because we carry a LOT. Gas and air cylinders (they are heavy), the big midwife bag (it's even heavier), and sometimes the birthing pool things too. Parking three streets away and walking back and forth with all that means more time away from you. And our arms are tired!

---

## Parking permits (Anfield, Kensington and other permit zones)

If you live in a **permit parking zone**, like parts of Anfield or Kensington, please sort out a **visitor permit** before your baby is due. You can ask the council about this.

Then leave the permit somewhere easy, by the front door or ready to hand straight to us, so we can put it on the dashboard.

We have had parking tickets before while we were busy helping a baby into the world. It's not a nice present to come back to!

---

## Help us find your door

This is the big one. Sat navs are clever, but they are not perfect. Here are some real things that have happened to us:

**The flats.** One midwife drove round a block of flats in Everton for 20 minutes. Flat 13 was in one building. Flat 14 was in a completely different building. In the end, the dad leaned out the window and waved a tea towel until she saw him. It worked, but let's not make it a tradition.

**The house with a name.** Another time, a house had no number, only a lovely name, in a street of terraced houses. The sat nav took the midwife to the chippy. Nice smell, wrong place.

**The wrong house.** And once, one of us walked into the wrong house because the door was open. A very nice older gentleman was sitting there. He gave her a Jammie Dodger anyway. Very kind, but still the wrong house.

So, to save time (and biscuits), please help us:

### Send us a pin
- **Send your location on WhatsApp** to the birth line phone, or
- Use **what3words**. It gives your exact spot using three words. It's very good, honestly.

### If you live in flats
- Tell us **which building** and **which entrance**
- Tell us the **door code** or how to get in
- If the flat numbers are confusing, tell us! You know your building better than anyone.

### If your house has a name and no number
- Tell us the **nearest numbered house** or a landmark ("next to the corner shop", "opposite the church")

### Make your house easy to spot
- **Turn the porch light on at night, please!** In winter, dark streets all look the same.
- Put something on the gate or door. One family tied **balloons** to their gate like it was a party. Best idea ever. We found them straight away. (And it was a party, really. A birthday!)
- A big sign in the window with your house number works too.

---

## Getting inside

Once we're at the door, we want to get to you quickly and safely, carrying all our heavy things.

### Clear the way
Please keep the **hallway and stairs clear**. That means:
- No shoes
- No washing basket
- No Lego (nobody should step on Lego, but especially not a midwife carrying a gas cylinder)
- No bags, prams or bikes in the way if you can help it

### Pets, please, in another room
We love animals, we really do. But during labour, and especially during the pushing, please put your pets in **another room** with the door shut.

One very friendly Staffie loved one of our midwives so much he jumped on her at every visit. We won't say his name. He knows who he is. She nearly dropped the Entonox (that's the gas and air)!

Your dog or cat will be happier somewhere calm, and we can concentrate on you and your baby.

---

## Who's opening the door?

When we're on our way, decide **who will let us in**. If you're in labour, it shouldn't be you running down the stairs!

Your birth partner, a friend or a family member can watch for us, open the door, and show us where to go.

---

## Last word from us

We know this is a lot to think about. You don't have to be perfect. Babies come when they come, and we will always do our very best to get to you.

But a little bit of planning now makes a big difference when the time comes. A porch light, a WhatsApp pin, a clear hallway and a dog behind a door can save us precious minutes.

We're looking forward to meeting your baby. See you soon, hopefully at the right house!

**With love,**
**The Riverside Community Midwives**

---

## ✂️ Fridge Checklist: Ready for Your Midwives

*Cut this out and stick it on the fridge. Tick when done!*

**Before the big day**
☐ I know home birth cover starts at **37 weeks**
☐ I know to go to the **hospital** if labour starts **before 37 weeks**
☐ The **Birth Line number** is saved in my phone AND my partner's phone: [BIRTH LINE NUMBER]
☐ I have sorted a **visitor parking permit** (if I live in a permit zone)
☐ I have my **what3words** or know how to send a **WhatsApp pin**
☐ I have written down my **door code / building / entrance** (if I live in flats)
☐ I have something to make my house easy to spot (balloons, sign, ribbon!)
☐ I have decided **who will open the door**

**When labour starts**
☐ Ring the **Birth Line**, not the midwife's own mobile
☐ Send our **location pin** to the birth line phone
☐ **Porch light ON** (if it's dark)
☐ **Two parking spaces** free if possible
☐ Visitor permit **ready by the door**
☐ **Hallway and stairs clear** (no shoes, no washing, no Lego!)
☐ **Pets in another room**, door shut
☐ Front door ready to open when we arrive

**In an emergency, ring 999.**

---

A few quick notes for you before it goes out:

- **Numbers:** I've left **[BIRTH LINE NUMBER]** as a placeholder. Add the hospital number too if it's not already clear in their notes.
- **999 line:** That wasn't in your notes, but it felt wrong to leave it off a home birth handout. Check with Deb that the wording matches what your team tells families.
- **Privacy:** Because this goes on Facebook, I didn't name the Staffie or use "Rosemary Cottage", in case the family is recognised. You can put them back if they're happy with that.
- It's about 1,350 words. That's on the long side for one folder page, so it may need two sides or smaller text.
